lead: An NMOS inverter is one nMOS driver that pulls the output down plus a load that pulls it up. The driver alone cannot make a logic 1, so the load sets the high level, and because the load is still on when the driver pulls down, the low level is a tug-of-war between the two. Four loads are standard: a resistor, an enhancement nMOS with its gate at V<sub>DD</sub>, a depletion nMOS with its gate tied to its source, and a pMOS with its gate at ground (pseudo-nMOS). Each gives a different V<sub>OH</sub>, V<sub>OL</sub> and static current; the idea survives today as ratioed logic.
prereq: You need: the five-region analysis of the CMOS inverter and the body effect on threshold voltage (see Threshold voltage and body effect).

sections.h3: The load line and the resistive load

blocks.text: With a resistor R<sub>L</sub> from V<sub>DD</sub> to the output, the load current (V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>out</sub>)/R<sub>L</sub> is a straight load line on the driver's I-V curves, and each input picks the crossing. With V<sub>in</sub> = 0 the driver is off and V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>. With V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>, V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>OL</sub> is far below V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>, so the driver is linear:
(VDD − VOL)/RL = kn[(VDD − Vtn)VOL − VOL²/2] Here kn = µnCox(W/L) is the driver gain in A/V². The left side is the resistor current and the right side the linear-region driver current.
A small low level needs a large R<sub>L</sub>, and a 100 kΩ resistor is far larger than a transistor, so it was replaced by a transistor load.

Enhancement load. An nMOS with drain and gate at VDD and source at the output. Its VGS = VDS = VDD − Vout, so it is always saturated while on. It stops conducting when VGS falls to its threshold, so VOH = VDD − Vt,load. The load's source is the output, so VSB = Vout and the body effect raises Vt,load and lowers VOH further. At Vin = VDD:
(kL/2)(VDD − VOL − Vt)² = kD[(VDD − Vt)VOL − VOL²/2] Here kL and kD are the load and driver gains. VOL depends on the ratio kD/kL, so the driver must be several times stronger.

Depletion load. An nMOS with an extra channel implant has a negative threshold −Vtd, so with its gate tied to its source (VGS = 0) it is always on. With the driver off, the only consistent state is zero load current, which needs VDS = 0: VOH = VDD, a full high level. While saturated it pulls up with a nearly constant current IDSS = (kL/2)Vtd². The body effect makes Vtd smaller as the output rises, so this current falls somewhat near the top of the swing. The constant-current pull-up charges the load faster than an enhancement load; the price is one more process step.

Pseudo-nMOS. A pMOS load with source at VDD, drain at the output and gate at ground is always on, so VOH = VDD. With the driver on, the pMOS is saturated as long as VOL ≤ |Vtp|, and then (kp/2)(VDD − |Vtp|)² = kn[(VDD − Vtn)VOL − VOL²/2]. It needs no extra process step in a CMOS process, which is why it survives; it is worked with numbers in the chapter on ratioed logic.
All four draw current whenever the output is low, which the CMOS inverter avoids. They are ratioed: the low level depends on a ratio of strengths, not on absolute sizes.

examples.question: A resistive-load NMOS inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, R<sub>L</sub> = 100 kΩ, driver k<sub>n</sub> = 20 µA/V² and V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.8 V. The input is at 5 V. Find V<sub>OL</sub> and the static power.
steps: The driver is on (V<sub>GS</sub> = 5 V > 0.8 V). If it were saturated it would carry (20/2) × (4.2)² = 176.4 µA, which would drop 17.6 V across R<sub>L</sub>, more than V<sub>DD</sub>. So it is linear.

Equate (5 − V<sub>OL</sub>)/100 kΩ = 20 µA/V² × [4.2V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2]. Multiply by 100 kΩ: 5 − V<sub>OL</sub> = 8.4V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>², so V<sub>OL</sub>² − 9.4V<sub>OL</sub> + 5 = 0.
V<sub>OL</sub> = (9.4 − √(88.36 − 20))/2 = (9.4 − 8.268)/2 = 0.566 V. The other root, 8.83 V, is above V<sub>DD</sub> and is rejected.
Check: 0.566 V < 4.2 V, so the linear assumption holds.
Static current I = (5 − 0.566)/100 kΩ = 44.3 µA; static power = 5 V × 44.3 µA = 0.22 mW.
examples.answer: V<sub>OL</sub> ≈ 0.57 V; the gate draws 44.3 µA, 0.22 mW, all the time its output is low.

examples.question: An enhancement-load inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, V<sub>t</sub> = 0.8 V for both transistors (ignore body effect), k<sub>L</sub> = 20 µA/V² and k<sub>D</sub> = 180 µA/V² (ratio 9). Find V<sub>OH</sub>, V<sub>OL</sub> and the static current at the low output.
steps: At V<sub>in</sub> = 5 V the load is saturated and the driver linear: (20/2)(4.2 − V<sub>OL</sub>)² = 180[4.2V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2] (currents in µA).

Divide by 10: (4.2 − V<sub>OL</sub>)² = 18(4.2V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2) = 75.6V<sub>OL</sub> − 9V<sub>OL</sub>². Expand: 17.64 − 8.4V<sub>OL</sub> + V<sub>OL</sub>² = 75.6V<sub>OL</sub> − 9V<sub>OL</sub>², so 10V<sub>OL</sub>² − 84V<sub>OL</sub> + 17.64 = 0.
examples.answer: V<sub>OH</sub> = 4.2 V (lower still with body effect), V<sub>OL</sub> ≈ 0.22 V, and 159 µA flows while the output is low.

traps: Using the saturation equation for the driver at the low output. V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>OL</sub> is far below V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>, so the driver is linear.
Giving V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> for the enhancement load. It stops one threshold short, and the body effect makes that threshold larger than V<sub>t0</sub>.
Calling a depletion load off because V<sub>GS</sub> = 0. Its threshold is negative, so it conducts until V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.
Taking the supply side as the source of an nMOS load. Its source is the output, so its V<sub>GS</sub> and V<sub>SB</sub> follow the output.

quiz.q: Name the four loads used with an NMOS inverter and the drawback all four share.
quiz.a: Resistor, enhancement nMOS, depletion nMOS and pMOS (pseudo-nMOS). All draw static current whenever the output is low.

quiz.q: Why is the high output of an enhancement-load inverter V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>t</sub> and not V<sub>DD</sub>?
quiz.a: The load gate is at V<sub>DD</sub> and its source is the output, so V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>out</sub>. With the driver off the current must fall to zero, which happens at V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>t</sub>, so V<sub>out</sub> stops at V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>t</sub>; body effect raises V<sub>t</sub> and lowers it further.

quiz.q: A depletion load has V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 at all times, yet the output high reaches V<sub>DD</sub>. Explain.
quiz.a: Its threshold is negative, so it conducts at V<sub>GS</sub> = 0. With the driver off, zero current is reached only when V<sub>DS</sub> = 0, that is V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>.

quiz.q: A depletion-load inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, I<sub>DSS</sub> = 20 µA, driver k<sub>n</sub> = 100 µA/V² and V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.8 V. Find V<sub>OL</sub>.
How does the VTC of a pseudo-nMOS inverter differ from a CMOS inverter, and what does that do to the noise margins?
quiz.a: The weak always-on pull-up makes the curve asymmetric: V<sub>M</sub> sits well below V<sub>DD</sub>/2 and V<sub>OL</sub> is above 0 V. NM<sub>H</sub> stays large, but NM<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>IL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub> is small, so a low input is easily disturbed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Depletion-load NMOS was the process of the classic 8-bit and 16-bit microprocessors before CMOS took over in the 1980s. Ratioed pull-ups live on in keepers and in the wide NOR planes of PLAs and ROMs. Search next for depletion-load NMOS logic.

figure.caption: The four pull-ups of an NMOS inverter over the same nMOS driver, with the levels from this chapter's examples at V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V. Only the enhancement load loses a threshold at the top; every one fights the driver when the output is low.
